paragraphs: The edict was written twice in Chengming Hall.

The first draft came quickly. As the Secretariat drafter set brush to paper, Fu Jian paced before the map. He stopped only once, to order the words *southern expedition* struck out and replaced with *preparations for defense on the southern frontier*.

The drafter dared ask neither whom they were preparing against nor how far that defense was to extend. He scraped the tip of his brush gently against the inkstone and wrote that three hundred thousand men would be summoned from Guanzhong, Hebei, Heluo, Xiangyang, and the frontier provinces to assemble at Luoyang and drill in formations on land and water, in readiness for the southern border.
Fu Jian read it and stamped the Heavenly King’s seal at the end.
The vermilion paste was still wet when Crown Prince Fu Hong arrived.
“Father truly means to summon three hundred thousand?”
“I had you debate it all day yesterday. The court has reached no conclusion about war. What is wrong with drilling first at Luoyang?”
“The old Hebei garrisons are stretched with rotating guard duty. Spring grass has only just appeared in Hexi. If the cavalry moves south, the trade routes will need fresh escorts.”
“That is why the central military headquarters must examine the order.”

Fu Hong looked at the sheet, his gaze resting briefly on the two characters meaning *defense*. He said nothing more. Fu Jian had almost hoped his son would ask more questions. Only yesterday they had disputed openly before a hundred officials. Now there were just the two of them, and the boy seemed to have lost even the heart to argue.
“You fear I will break my pledge to Wang Jinglüe?”
“I fear that once the army reaches Luoyang, people will say it cannot be sent home.”
Fu Jian frowned. “I have said nothing about marching south.”

Fu Hong bowed his head. The edict then went to the central military headquarters, while the Secretariat received its customary copy. The vermilion seal was genuine. So were the three hundred thousand written on the paper. But at this stage the document remained a draft mobilization order awaiting verification: the Heavenly King’s seal alone did not authorize the provinces to dispatch troops.

Murong Chui received the document in the military headquarters courtyard. As a young clerk read aloud the words “three hundred thousand,” he was having several broken straps removed from training armor. Since the battle on the snowy plains of Hexi, he had ceased to believe that a handsome formation revealed everything about an army. Some men stood straight in armor yet, after a march of three hundred *li*, scarcely had shoes left on their feet.
“Are the representatives of all the provinces here?” he asked.
“They are. The men from Hebei have brought fresh garrison rolls.”
“Send them in.”

A deputy commander from the Hebei military administration first spread out the numbers assigned to posts between Ye and the places northeast of Luoyang. Red dots on the register marked districts where great families of the former Yan had settled. Murong Chui showed no emotion. He knew the names. He had once drunk wine in some of those courtyards; men from other households had held his horse when he served Yan. Their sons could no longer even name the emperor of those years, but they still remembered the little old Yan flags their fathers had hidden in holes in the walls.
“Seventy thousand cannot be withdrawn,” the deputy said.
Fu Pi sat to one side, representing the headquarters that trained the southern fleet. He looked up at once. “Hebei has troops enough. Why must Guanzhong alone supply the men?”
“Your Highness, Guanzhong does not have Ye, the old seat of another dynasty. If we take seventy thousand at once, whom will its remaining guards ask for help?”
“The districts can supply replacements.”
“The districts' available men are already marked on yellow slips. Move them into the garrisons and the spring planting and grain convoys will be short of hands first.”

Fu Pi frowned. He had brought more than slogans this time. The reports from Xiangyang set out shipyards, crews, and grain transport in full figures. To hear every northern district say it could spare no soldiers before his army even reached the Huai sent a chill through him.
Murong Chui lifted a hand to stop them. “Hebei will send thirty thousand: ten thousand cavalry and twenty thousand foot. If the Heavenly King asks who proposed the reduction, put down my name.”
The deputy commander breathed easier. Fu Pi asked, “Without the other men, how will the eastern army exert its strength?”
“By keeping the cities it must defend secure.”

Next the Hexi headquarters argued that the trade routes had only recently been brought under control and its garrisons could not be emptied. Reports from Bingzhou warned of frequent raiders beyond the frontier. Officers at Xiangyang said the newly repaired Han River crossings were already defended by too few men. The grain ledger Fu Rong had sent specially was terser than any of their arguments. On one rough sheet it set out how much grain Luoyang needed for three months, how many wagons each posting station from Guanzhong could provision, and how much market grain the ordinary people of Heluo depended upon to live.

The commanders argued into the afternoon. The cold meal in the courtyard had been replaced once already. Every province wished to contribute men and win distinction in a future southern campaign, yet feared its own northern defenses would fail the moment its best soldiers were gone. An old Guanzhong general asked, “If we contend for all under heaven in the south, does the north cease to be part of all under heaven?” The courtyard suddenly fell silent. Fu Pi grimly rolled up the naval chart in his sleeve.

The military headquarters finally agreed that, for the present, 153,000 men could be assembled at Luoyang for no more than three months. The other provinces would retain their existing defenses. The army was forbidden to advance south of the Ru River. The headquarters would separately list how many days each unit needed to return to its post; neither the original military rolls nor the garrison-farming rotations could be altered without authorization. Murong Chui signed the recommendation himself and stamped the military headquarters' seal beneath its verification. The opinion was sent back to Chengming Hall, asking the Secretariat to draft anew on that basis. They would not place their second seal upon the original order for three hundred thousand.
Fu Jian read two pages, his expression quiet throughout.
“Three hundred thousand requested, and only a hundred and fifty-three thousand left?”

“I checked the numbers with the provincial commanders,” Murong Chui said. “Any more means drawing away border garrisons and the farmers tagged yellow. Reduce the defenders, and the moment trouble stirs in Hebei, the army newly arrived at Luoyang will have to turn back north.”
“Including the people of your former Yan?”
“Including them.”

Fu Jian looked up. When Wang Meng was alive, the two of them had argued until their faces reddened in Chengming Hall over Murong Chui’s military command. Now that Murong Chui himself had committed the grounds for suspicion to a formal opinion, Fu Jian found it harder to blame him.
“What can such an army accomplish?”
“It can drill, defend the frontier, and respond at once to fighting along the Huai.”
“And if the enemy comes north?”
“I ask leave to fight.”
“And if I wish it to continue south?”
Murong Chui met his eyes. “Then there must be a new campaign edict. The grain wagons and the towns left behind must be counted again.”

Fu Jian ordered the military headquarters' recommendation retained. At dawn the next day, a new draft bearing the Heavenly King’s authority was prepared: 153,000 men, assembly at Luoyang, three months' duration, no crossing south of the Ru River. But the Secretariat drafter left a gap in the provision on the end date, writing only, *At the appointed term, disposition shall be discussed in light of frontier conditions*. The words *attack Jin* were still absent.
Fu Jian read it and stamped his seal.

The officers of the central military headquarters checked the troop numbers and geographical limits once more, then affixed their seal to the new draft. It went on to the Secretariat. If the Secretariat added its seal, the provinces could use the same final text to issue military tallies, grain rations, and fodder for the horses.

Fu Hong sat in the hall for a long time. Orioles had called twice outside the window when the finance officers came in carrying their ledgers. They had feared the crown prince would find the questions too great for junior clerks to raise first. To their surprise, his first question was about grain.
“How many months can Luoyang support a hundred and fifty-three thousand?”
“Three. A little more if the roads are not badly delayed.”
“And spring planting behind them?”
“With the reductions proposed by the military headquarters, it can be maintained.”
“Can the mobilization order be issued?”
“Under today’s wording, the accounts can be verified.”

Having answered, the official looked troubled. Again and again his gaze returned to the last sentence of the edict: *At the appointed term, disposition shall be discussed in light of frontier conditions*. Since the great defeat along the Huai, everyone in the army knew the force of such words. If the frontier situation tightened, three months could become six. Units already at Luoyang might move south one camp after another. A new military order might require the three seals to be considered afresh, but with the troops already before the emperor, who would dare say they must not move?

Fu Hong summoned all the departments. They debated until dusk, when an official urged him, “Your Highness, the edict contains no procedural error. If you obstruct today’s mobilization only because you suspect His Majesty may change his mind later, the whole realm will condemn the Secretariat.”
“You are right,” Fu Hong replied.

Everyone was startled. The prince opened the register limiting the garrison’s stay at Luoyang. “But transport charges and grain stores have been approved for only three months. Not a single return date has been fixed. We send the men today; three months from now they are still in Luoyang. Who feeds them?”

The finance officer took the book and listed the boats and wagons needed for the return journey, along with the term for which civilian vessels might be requisitioned. If the troops did not return, grain prices along the route, civilian carts, and the provincial autumn levies would all require new accounts. Fu Hong did not challenge the edict by guessing at his father’s thoughts. He laid before the officials the return journey’s bill, which should have been written clearly from the beginning.
“Ask the central Secretariat whether every unit will return to its post at the end of the term if no new edict is issued.”
An official asked, “Your Highness will seal the order if that sentence is added?”

“Army rations need an end date,” Fu Hong said. “Write it today and the Secretariat will seal it today. Refuse to write it, and no one may open the granary gates on the promise that we will discuss it later.”

So at the foot of the document the Secretariat wrote its finding: the troop numbers, three months' grain, and remaining garrisons were sound; the arrangements for returning the troops remained unclear. Its seal would therefore be withheld, and the document returned for correction. Someone advised Fu Hong to send a chief clerk with it. Instead he picked up the wooden chest and carried it himself to Chengming Hall.

The palace seemed deeper at night than by day. Only two lamps burned beneath the corridor. The stone steps, still wet after rain, shone black. Fu Jian sat alone at his desk, fine red veins in his eyes. On seeing his son he asked first, “Are all three seals in place?”
“The Secretariat has not sealed it.”
Fu Jian’s outstretched hand stopped halfway. After a long pause he said, “Bring it here.”
Fu Hong laid the edict before him. At the beginning stood the Heavenly King’s seal and the military headquarters' seal, side by side. At the end remained a square of blank paper.
“Why?”

“Please add that, upon the expiry of the term, the troops are to return in stages to their registered garrisons unless a new edict bearing all three seals is issued. If they must go south, grain and civilian labor must be verified anew.”
Fu Jian looked up. “I have not said they must go south.”
“Precisely because Your Majesty has not said it, we ask that you state how this mobilization is to end.”
“Must I promise the Secretariat what will happen three months later every time I move a single camp?”

“There is already a rule for urgent relief in battle: headquarters may move one camp and complete verification within the prescribed period. An assembly of 153,000 men across provinces cannot be handled as an emergency order for one camp.”

Fu Jian pushed his brush aside. There was neither panic nor grandstanding righteousness in his son’s voice. That only made him angrier. A man who defied him could be taught a lesson. But here stood the son he had raised, blocking his way with rules he had himself established, and for a moment he could not find words fit to curse him.
“Fu Hong, you always think I write *defend the frontier* while secretly meaning *cross the river*.”
Fu Hong was silent.
“Answer me.”
“Yes.”
“You do not trust your father?”

“I trust that Father has not, at this moment, issued an edict for a southern campaign.” He raised his head. “But once the troops reach Luoyang, the generals will petition every day, and the autumn grain will flow there every day. Asking them to disband then will be harder for Father than it is today.”
Fu Jian’s face changed. “You are certain I will use an army already assembled to force the court’s hand?”
“I fear that no one will dare ask the army to return.”
“You dare.”
“I dare now.”

That final word struck home. Fu Jian sprang to his feet and slapped Fu Hong across the face. The crown prince staggered backward, catching the edge of the desk to steady himself. Blood appeared at the corner of his mouth and fell upon his robe, one very small drop. For a moment both men stood stunned. Fu Jian had not struck his son like that in years. He remembered the child’s first visit to the Secretariat, his hands trembling so badly under the edict scroll that he feared dropping the emperor’s seal. That child would now sooner be struck than put the final seal on his father’s order.
“Kneel.”
Fu Hong knelt. He did not wipe the blood from his face.
“Where is the seal?”
“In the chest.”
“Give it to me.”

Fu Hong presented the bronze seal with both hands. It was nowhere near so heavy as the great seal of the Heavenly King. Its knob shone faintly where years of fingers had worn it smooth. Fu Jian took it and moved it toward the blank space on the edict.

If he wished, he could remove the crown prince tonight and appoint another head of the Secretariat. Or he could openly declare the situation urgent, issue a special edict, and take responsibility for bypassing the procedure. The hundred and fifty thousand men would march. No one would stop them on the imperial road. But if he used this seal to pretend that the Secretariat agreed, every official would know tomorrow that the seal was present and the verification was gone.

He raised the seal toward the light. Along one corner ran a fine crack, made years earlier when a clerk in the grain department dropped it. Fu Hong had asked at the time whether it should be recast. Quan Yi had said there was no need, as long as its impression remained legible. Now almost everyone in the realm was urging him to raise an army, and this battered corner of bronze still seemed to remember the old questions at the granary gate.

Footsteps came from outside. Fu Rong and Murong Chui had heard the news and were waiting beyond the doors. Fu Pi had arrived too. When the attendant asked whether they should enter, Fu Jian closed his hand around the seal and summoned them in.

Fu Pi saw his younger brother kneeling at once. Alarm flickered across his face. He and Fu Hong argued constantly, but seeing the boy struck, his first words were, “What has he said this time? If Father intends to punish him, at least have the physician stop the bleeding first.”
“It is not your place to instruct me,” Fu Jian said.
Fu Pi withdrew toward the steps, but his hands were clenched tight. Fu Rong saw the empty space at the end of the edict and understood at once what had brought them there.
Yao Chang entered as well, last of all. He stopped beside the doorway and stood quietly after bowing. Fu Jian noticed him. “I did not summon you.”
“Your Majesty, I heard the troop order had not gone out. I feared that the rites for the army’s assembly at Luoyang, which fall under my ministry, might be mistimed. I dared not stay away.”
The reason lay within his office’s responsibilities. For a moment no one could object. Fu Jian paid him no further heed.

Fu Rong read the Secretariat’s opinion first and pointed to the phrase *Disposition shall be discussed in light of frontier conditions*. “If you refuse to write that the troops will return, then you must add six months of grain. The present registers allow only three. This cannot be passed over.”

Murong Chui nodded beside him. “The military headquarters verified a limited three-month assembly. The troops can practice formations at Luoyang. But once those three months have passed, the barracks will not grow their own grain merely because the banners are still standing.”
Fu Pi could not contain himself. “Do you forbid changes in the situation on a battlefield?”
“Of course not,” Murong Chui said. “When circumstances change, issue a new order.”
“What if the Jin army suddenly crosses the Huai?”

“The army is north of the Ru. Under the existing defensive rules, the nearest camps can move first. I will lead them against the enemy then. I need not wait until a clerk in Chang’an has finished writing.”
Fu Rong added, “But fear of a future emergency is no reason to send fifteen ten-thousands of men into camp without a final date for their grain.”

Only then did Yao Chang speak. He did not agitate or raise his voice. “Your Majesty, two seals are in place. Only one is lacking at the threshold. If a few words leave the armies unable to move, Jin will laugh at us. I suggest the Heavenly King issue a special edict in full daylight and decide, when the three months end, whether to advance or retreat as the occasion requires.”
Still kneeling, Fu Hong did not look at him. But Fu Jian asked, “Once the special edict is issued, what remains for the Secretariat to verify?”
“Ordinary military supplies can still be checked as before.”
“And the next time some matter of great importance arises?”
Yao Chang’s smile faded slightly. “Then too, we would ask Your Majesty to decide.”

It was the easiest road. Fu Jian knew it. In so many years of disorder, what powerful ruler had not taken it? Yet at Wang Meng’s sickbed he had written with his own hand that an army must no longer rest on the assumption that one man would always be trustworthy. If, merely to avoid adding a few words at the end of an edict, he slipped today around the bar he had fitted to his own door, who among his ministers would keep a seal locked in its chest the next time a verification was unwelcome?
He looked at Fu Hong. The red mark on the crown prince’s cheek had not yet faded. Nor had the anger in Fu Jian’s breast. Neither father nor son met the other’s eyes.
After a moment Fu Jian returned the Secretariat seal to the chest and closed its lid gently.
“Amend it according to the Secretariat’s opinion.”
No one in the hall had expected that answer. Fu Pi took half a step forward, then stopped.

Fu Jian turned to the Secretariat drafter. “Prepare a new final copy. One hundred and fifty-three thousand men, and not one more may be added without authorization. Assemble at Luoyang within three months to practice crossings and grain transport. Do not advance beyond the Ru River. At the end of the term, if there is no new military order bearing all three seals, return by stages to the garrisons according to the military headquarters' schedule. No district may requisition next year’s grain in the name of a southern expedition, nor recruit old followers anew.”

The clerk wrote more slowly than he had during the day. After each provision he stopped to read it aloud. Fu Rong checked the grain; Murong Chui checked the troops left to defend each province; Fu Pi checked one by one the numbers drawn from his naval force at Xiangyang. Not all his ships were included in the new order. He was disappointed, but no longer proposed adding them at the last moment.

Once the draft was revised, the three offices signed and stamped the final copy in order. Fu Jian placed the Heavenly King’s seal first. The central military headquarters checked the troop numbers again and added its own. When Fu Hong accepted the Secretariat seal, his hand still trembled a little, though not from fear. He read the clause on returning to the garrisons once more, checked even the grain reserved for several small towns in Bingzhou, and only then stamped the final space.
Disagreement among the three offices had forced the troop order to be recopied twice. When the last seal touched the paper, the red paste seeped into its fibers in a thin line.

Fu Jian looked at the three seals, feeling none of the relief his ministers might have expected. He had indeed cut three hundred thousand to 153,000 and confined what could have become an indefinitely extended assembly to three months. Yet 153,000 men would still march toward Luoyang. Xie An would surely hear of their formations in Heluo. The courts of both Chang’an and Jiankang would make new calculations because of them.
“That will be all tonight,” Fu Jian said.
As the others prepared to leave, he called Fu Hong back.
“Since the crown prince knows the Secretariat’s regulations so well, he may return to the Eastern Palace for the present and study them properly once more.”
Fu Hong was taken aback.

“The day-to-day affairs of the Secretariat will temporarily pass to the Vice Director of the Left. You are not to handle the Luoyang military order. You will resume your duties when I issue a further decree.”

Fu Rong began to speak, then stopped. Fu Pi looked at his brother, his face darker than it had been during the court debate. Fu Hong bowed his head to the floor and accepted the order. He had defended the blank space, but its cost could not be erased by the fact that his objection had been accepted.

Fu Jian dismissed them all and remained alone. He picked up the first order for three hundred thousand, bearing his own seal but now invalid, and held it beneath the lamp. Without the other two seals it had no force as a military order. He stared at that lonely red impression, remembering how many city gates had opened in surrender during his youth on the authority of that seal alone.
It was not that the gates no longer recognized his seal. He himself had built them stronger than before.

The next day the order for 153,000 men went out from Chang’an to the provinces. Wagons rumbled ceaselessly beyond the eastern gate. Couriers charged with military grain changed horses again and again in the morning mist. Watching the official carts, the people wondered whether this was truly a drill or the beginning of an expedition south. No one in the streets knew what had passed in Chengming Hall that night.

In the crown prince’s residence, Fu Hong held a cold cloth against his face. When Fu Rong came to see him, he heard the turning of pages before he reached the door. There was no wine and there were no visitors. Only an old register of casualties from the Huai campaign lay on the desk.
“Does it hurt?” Fu Rong asked.
“Not much now.”
“Once, beside Wang Meng’s bed, that father of yours would not let a single sentence stand in his way. Today you have learned what that felt like.”
Fu Hong smiled, tugged at the corner of his sore mouth, and frowned again.
Fu Rong asked, “Do you regret it?”

“Uncle, when I placed the seal today, several chief clerks of the Secretariat examined the text even more closely than I did,” Fu Hong said. “One who is afraid of everything dared say, right in front of the Secretariat drafter, that the final date for grain supplies could not be left vague.”
“That is no bad thing.”
“No.” Fu Hong put the cold cloth back in the bronze basin. “When I am no longer in the Secretariat, they will still know how to read that line.”

Fu Rong asked no more. He pushed the window open a little for his nephew. Outside, the spring wind had bent the willow branches low over the wall. On the imperial road toward Luoyang, the first train of ox-carts carrying army grain had already left Guanzhong.
The court said the soldiers would return to their original garrisons in three months.
No one yet knew what news would come north from the lands beyond the Yangtze within those three months.
